newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan central depository seen boosting turnover.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan central depository seen boosting turnover.

text.p: Pakistan's three stock exchanges will be hooked to a Central Depository System (CDS) on September 3, but some brokers say adjusting to it may take time.

Some worry about job losses in a computerised environment, some say the perceived threat of documentation might drive away investors who find advantages in secrecy. Others fret about practical questions: what happens if there is a power cut, or fire?
The new system's defenders say it will transform an outdated settlement culture, reassure foreign investors and boost volume.
"The CDS will bring efficiency and transparency in the delivery, settlement and transfer of shares," said Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) President Arif Habib.
"Generally brokers and investors have welcomed it, but at the same time there is a fear of the unknown among some members because it's a new concept."

The system, set up by the Central Depository Company (CDC) at a cost of more than 200 million rupees ($4.9 million), will eliminate physical settlement of securities and introduce an electronic computerised book entry system.
The CDC, in which the Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad stock exchanges have equity stakes, announced on Tuesday that it would start operating on September 3.
"Physical handling of shares was a major problem. It hampered growth in trading volume. After the central depository begins working, turnover will increase," Habib said.
Najam Ali, the CDC's chief executive officer, said the system was needed to develop Pakistan's capital market.
"Foreign investors have expressed concern about our settlement procedures. Many are reluctant to enter because they think they are exposed to certain risks," Ali said.
"The central depository will end these risks. I expect a lot of foreign investment once it is operational."
Many brokers and agents harbour reservations about the new system, saying it could cost jobs in the settlement department.
Habib said surplus staff would be needed in other departments because the CDC would boost the overall business.
"For educated people there will be opportunities in research and marketing. But for uneducated people, opportunities will shrink. Older people will have to get accustomed to computers."
CDC officials acknowledge that it may take a couple of years for Pakistani bourses to assimilate a new settlement culture.
"We don't want to move fast. The system may not work if we try to impose it. We will implement it gradually," Ali said.
In the first phase, the CDC plans to register 50 companies by next June, out of 782 listed at the KSE.

"We can't include all the listed companies in one go, but we will have all the highly traded companies as soon as posible. It will take at least another two years to take all the companies under our umbrella," Ali said.

"We will quickly register all the companies at the CDC if people feel comfortable with the system. But if we face resistance on the part of account-holders or companies, then this would be a difficult target," he added.
Habib said Pakistan had a large "black" economy and there were concerns that the CDC would discourage stock investment.

"But our system has taken these issues into account. It covers foreign investors as well as the requirement of local individuals and institutions. Those owners who don't want to disclose names can operate through group accounts," he said.
Brokers say the CDC will eliminate the risk of forgery and theft of shares, but its computer and communication systems could be prey to Pakistan's long and frequent power cuts.
Habib said the CDC had ensured an uninterrupted power supply for its computer and communication network, but account-holders would have to arrange for a back-up power supply.
KSE officials said a few companies had expressed concern about the safety of share-holder records in case of disaster.
"We will explain to them there are no undue risks. In case of a disaster like fire, we have contingency plans and arrangements," Ali said.
"Users should have faith in the entire system, which is not just software and hardware," he said. A marketing effort would be launched to convince the industry to accept the CDS concept.
